_about: Curated SHIELD-AI -> NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 crosswalk (all seven pillars). DRAFT: AI-assisted, NOT yet reviewed by a control SME. Source of truth for oscal/shield-ai-to-800-53r5-mapping.json (built by tools/generate_oscal_crosswalk.py). Matching rationale is 'functional' (NIST IR 8477). Direction: source = SHIELD-AI control, target = 800-53 control; 'subset-of' means every SHIELD requirement is within the 800-53 target.

_fit_values.direct: An org meeting the mapped 800-53 controls, with agents in scope as subjects and sensible ODPs, substantially meets the SHIELD control. No residual requirement.
_fit_values.partial: The core of the control maps to 800-53, but SHIELD adds requirements 800-53 does not state. Residual is recorded.
_fit_values.novel: Only tangential 800-53 analogues exist. The control's main idea is new relative to 800-53.

findings: **Human approval of autonomous action (IAM-03) is the notable IAM gap.** It is central to agent safety yet the nearest 800-53 controls are AC-4.9 (information flows) and AC-3.2 (dual authorization), neither scoped to actions. The NIST cross-check below found no NIST control for it either, and NIST publicly cautions about relying on it.

**Keyword matching would mislead.** IAM-10 'taint-tracking' collides with SI-20 'Tainting', a different concept (exfiltration detection). It is recorded as `no-relationship` with a blocking qualifier. Tooling that auto-maps on titles or text similarity would get this wrong.

**One identity tension (IAM-01 vs IA-2).** IA-2 ties a process to the user it acts for; IAM-01 requires a distinct agent identity. Compatible, but an implementation that reads IA-2 literally could satisfy it while failing IAM-01. Recorded as a qualifier. TP-02 inherits the same dependency (the tool must authenticate the agent, not the human).

**TP: mechanism maps, trigger does not.** The later TP controls (TP-10 to TP-16) come from incidents where an agent or its tooling is induced to execute attacker-controlled instructions or code. The mechanism half (signing, input validation, allow-listing, process isolation, provenance) has 800-53 homes. The trigger half (content the agent reads becomes a command; the model is an instruction source whose output must be authenticated) does not.

**TP-11 is the clearest novel control in the pillar.** Treating rendered content as a command channel and preserving origin isolation for an acting agent has no 800-53 vocabulary. A keyword search of Rev 5.2 statements and guidance for 'same-origin' returned no hits and for 'browser' one incidental hit. The targets listed are tangential.

**One 800-53 control, two different fits (SI-10.6).** Its mechanism (parameterized interfaces, output escaping) presumes a data/code boundary. TP-16 has one (an OS launch path), so SI-10.6 fits well. TP-04 does not: an LLM context has no such boundary, so the same control gives weak cover. Recorded as a qualifier on TP-04.

**TP-15: 800-53 permits the weak reading.** SC-39 (separate execution domain per process) arguably excludes an in-process denylist sandbox, but never says so; an assessor could accept a hardened interpreter as an 'execution domain'. SHIELD-AI's value here is the explicit negative.

**Supply-chain controls transfer best.** TP-05, TP-13 and TP-14 map onto the SR family, CM-14 and SI-7.15, where 800-53's provenance and authenticity vocabulary predates agent skill marketplaces but still applies. The residual is that the payload is natural-language instructions and runtime-fetchable instruction channels, not just code.
**TP-07 is a borderline partial/novel.** RA-3 and SA-11.2 would cover analysis of tool composition only if the organisation chose to scope threat modelling that way; nothing in 800-53 asks for it.

**Coverage tracks how generic the control is.** The governance, monitoring and incident-response controls map best because 800-53's PM, CA, AU and IR families are technology-neutral and apply to AI systems unchanged. The novel controls cluster where the model itself is the attack surface (MS-07, MS-09, MS-14), with IAM-07, IAM-10, TP-11 and GRM-03 as the others. MS-04 was first rated novel and was reclassified to partial by the NIST cross-check.

**800-53 Rev 5.2 has no vocabulary for AI as a thing to be secured.** A keyword search of non-withdrawn statements and guidance finds no hits for 'training data', 'poison', 'tenant', 'ethic', 'autonom', 'human oversight' or 'playbook'. 'Artificial intelligence' appears only in RA-3.4 and SI-3, as a detection technique. A missing word is evidence of a vocabulary gap, not proof of no coverage.

**Integrity controls do not detect authorised poison.** MS-02 (training data), MS-10 (agent memory) and MS-13 (transcripts) all involve data that is written through a legitimate path. SI-7 and SR-4 detect unauthorised change and provenance breaks; a malicious but authorised write is neither. An organisation could report SI-7 as met while the threat is untouched. Recorded as a qualifier on MS-02.

**Human approval of agent action is a recurring gap, not a single one.** IAM-03 (approval before high-risk action), TP-12 (approval bound to the exact call), MS-09 (fidelity of what the approver sees) and DS-07 (approval the agent cannot trigger) all rest on a human-in-the-loop concept that 800-53 lacks. The nearest controls (AC-4.9, AC-3.2, AC-5) are written for information flows and for people.

**MS-07 pushes the opposite way from 800-53's test-environment controls.** CM-4.1 and SA-3.1 require test environments to be separate and protected; nothing asks that they be undetectable. An organisation can satisfy CM-4.1 with an obviously labelled test environment that a model can recognise. Recorded as a qualifier.

**DS-08: the egress that matters may leave from the client.** SC-7.5 and SC-7.10 govern the network boundary, but a rendered image tag or link unfurl is fetched by the user's client or a third-party service. SC-31 covert channel analysis is the best fit, but it is a design-time analysis, so it does not by itself keep an emergent-channel inventory current.

**MIR-03 creates a privacy obligation.** AU-14 requires consultation with legal counsel and AU-3.3 ties retained PII to a privacy risk assessment. A full prompt/response log is a new sensitive data store, so the control cannot be considered met without that assessment. Recorded as a qualifier.

**Governance controls rate direct only if AI is in scope.** GRM-01, GRM-04 and GRM-05 map to organisation-level controls (PM-29, SA-9, CA-7). An existing programme meets them only if it already covers AI systems and AI vendors; 800-53 does not require that.

**The privacy mappings are PII-scoped.** DS-04 and DS-05 rely on 800-53's privacy controls (PT, SI-12, PM-25), which concern personal data. DS-04 extends to all sensitive data in a context window, and DS-05 to training data in general. Alignment with the Privacy Act 1988 and the Australian Privacy Principles is not assessed here.

**'Novel' means novel to 800-53 as written, not to NIST's thinking.** In the NIST material searched, most novel controls' threats or principles appear as attack descriptions, research defences or stakeholder positions, but none appears as a control requirement. NIST's stated method for closing such gaps is the overlay: tailoring existing controls with organisation-defined parameters and discussion text (for example its SI-03(08) tailoring for predictive AI). Some partial and novel ratings may therefore become direct once an agent overlay (NISTIR 8605D) exists. None was published when this cross-check was done.

**NIST is publicly cautious about human-in-the-loop, which sharpens the IAM-03 gap rather than closing it.** SP 2400-102 says human-in-the-loop oversight is 'difficult to apply at the speed and scale at which agentic systems operate' and calls balancing escalation 'an open research problem'. A NIST blog likens approval overload to MFA fatigue, and NCCoE commenters recommend reserving human approval for high-impact actions. IAM-03 requires approval for high-risk actions and uses risk-based tiers at L3, which is that posture. The SHIELD-AI control schema does not discuss approval fatigue (searched all 69 controls for fatigue, habituation, rubber-stamping and approval volume, rate or quality). Approval quality, not only approval presence, is worth adding to IAM-03 and MS-09.

**Absence-of-term evidence is weak.** The 'not found' results are term searches over four NIST documents, run on text extracted from PDFs and web pages. A concept can be present under different wording, and a draft taxonomy is not NIST's complete position. Treat 'not found' as a prompt to look, not as proof.

EE-01.fit_basis: SC-39/SC-7.21/SC-24 cover isolation and failure behaviour; the prescriptive container-era requirements are not in 800-53.
EE-01.residual: No shared host mounts/IPC/network namespaces and immutable infrastructure are prescriptive technical requirements. 800-53 leaves them to ODPs; no 800-53 control names immutable infrastructure (closest: CM-2, CM-6, SI-7).

mappings.why: Separate execution domain per process is the generic form of one sandbox per agent.
Boundary mechanisms isolating supporting components; sandbox boundary is one such mechanism.
Fail in a known state covers the 'fail-closed on isolation breach' clause only.
Baseline configuration is the nearest home for the immutable-infrastructure clause; it does not require immutability.

EE-02.fit_basis: Default-deny, explicit-registration access to infrastructure APIs is access enforcement and least privilege applied to an agent subject. AC-6 explicitly covers 'processes acting on behalf of users'.

mappings.why: Enforcing approved authorizations for access to infrastructure APIs.
No implicit access beyond what the registered tool requires is least privilege.
Deny-by-default is network-level in 800-53; EE-02 is API-level. Related, not equivalent.

EE-03.fit_basis: Per-agent CPU/memory/network/storage/API-rate quotas are resource allocation (SC-6) with alerting (SI-4). Agent-as-insider framing is new but the mechanism is not.

mappings.why: Allocating resources by quota is the core requirement.
Resource exhaustion/DoS; SC-5 is oriented to external DoS events, EE-03 also covers a compromised agent as the source.
Alerting when limits are exceeded is a monitoring function.

EE-04.fit_basis: Isolation of evaluation from production maps to CM-4.1/SA-3.1. The 'model must not distinguish evaluation from production' requirement has no analogue.
EE-04.residual: Requirement that models must not be able to distinguish evaluation from production (links to MS-07) has no 800-53 analogue.

mappings.why: Analyse changes in a separate test environment before production.
Protect preproduction environments commensurate with risk.

EE-05.fit_basis: Write-path restriction and integrity monitoring map to CM-5 and SI-7; the specific attack class (agent writes a file the host later trusts and executes) is not named.
EE-05.residual: Agent-writable paths the host later loads as trusted configuration (shell profiles, IDE config, cron, systemd units). 800-53 has no control for this write-then-execute-as-trusted path.

mappings.why: Logical access restrictions on changes to the system.
Integrity verification tools (the filesystem integrity monitoring clause).
Allow-by-exception for what may execute; adjacent to the write-path allowlist.

EE-06.fit_basis: Verify the strongest isolation mode at runtime (SI-6), halt and alert rather than degrade (SC-24, SI-17). With ODPs set to 'halt agent execution' this is fully expressible.

mappings.why: Fail in a known state; EE-06 specifies the state (halted, alerting).
Verify correct operation of security functions and alert on failure.
Fail-safe procedures when failures occur.

EE-07.fit_basis: Restricting who can change security configuration is core 800-53 (CM-5, AC-6.1). The agent-era attack classes it lists are not.
EE-07.residual: Self-configuration poisoning by the agent, MCP registry entries as auto-run launch commands, and repository-supplied VCS config executing before the workspace-trust boundary are agent-era attack classes 800-53 does not name.

mappings.why: Enforce access restrictions associated with changes to the system.
Authorize access to security functions; the agent must not hold it for its own controls.
Configuration change control and approval.
Documented, approved configuration settings and deviations.

EE-08.fit_basis: The environment-separation core maps to CM-4.1; the active verification, target collision-checking and cross-run separation are the substance and are not in 800-53.
EE-08.residual: Active egress test before and during runs, collision-checking evaluation targets against real domains, and cryptographic separation of runs to prevent cross-run contamination are not in 800-53.

mappings.why: Separate test environments.
Protecting preproduction environments.
Verifying a control is operating, here by active test, is related to function verification.

IAM-01.fit_basis: Unique, auditable identity for an agent is identifier management for a non-person entity; IA-13 names NPEs. One tension to flag, recorded as a qualifier on IA-2.

mappings.why: Identifiers may be assigned to an individual, group, role, service or device; uniqueness is required.
Identity providers managing non-person entity (NPE) identities: the closest 800-53 term for agents.
Uniquely identify and authenticate services before communications.
Audit records carry the identity of the subject, which is how actions are attributed to an agent.
Associates the user's identification with processes acting for them. See qualifier.

qualifiers.subject: both
qualifiers.description: IA-2 binds a process to the identity of the user it acts for; IAM-01 requires an agent identity distinct from the human's. These are compatible if the agent has its own identity and a delegation link to the user, but an implementer who satisfies IA-2 by letting agents run under the user's identity would fail IAM-01.

IAM-02.fit_basis: Least privilege and no self-escalation are AC-6/AC-3. Agent-to-agent delegation limits are not addressed.
IAM-02.residual: Constraint that an agent cannot grant other agents permissions beyond its own scope. 800-53 has no delegation-of-privilege concept.

mappings.why: Least privilege for processes acting on behalf of users.
Enforcing approved authorizations, including no self-escalation.
Attribute-based policy is one way to express per-agent tool/data scope.

IAM-03.fit_basis: 800-53 has no general requirement for human approval of autonomous action. AC-4.9 (information flows) and AC-3.2 (dual authorization) are the nearest, and neither is scoped to agent actions. Central agentic concept with weak coverage.
IAM-03.residual: Human approval before high-risk autonomous agent actions is the central concept and has no direct 800-53 control. AC-4.9 is scoped to information flows; AC-3.2 is dual authorization between people.

mappings.why: Human reviews under defined conditions; scoped to information flows, not arbitrary actions.
Separation of duties covers the 'agent cannot approve its own action' clause.
Protecting authenticators; covers the gateway/operator token clause.
Dual authorization; a human approval gate is similar in shape but not in definition.

IAM-04.fit_basis: Authenticator management applies to agents. The explicit separation of agent and human credential stores and rotation domains is not required.
IAM-04.residual: Separate storage, management and rotation of agent versus human credentials, so that compromise of one does not compromise the other.

mappings.why: Authenticator management: storage, protection, change.
Protection of authenticators commensurate with the access they grant.

IAM-05.fit_basis: Ephemeral, auto-expiring credentials are IA-5 lifetime management plus AC-2.2 automatic removal of temporary accounts, given suitable ODPs.

mappings.why: Automatically remove or disable temporary accounts after a defined period.
Authenticator lifetime and refresh.
Prohibits use of cached authenticators after a period; related to stale-credential replay.

IAM-06.fit_basis: SC-4 and AC-4.21 supply the isolation vocabulary. Whether an LLM context window or memory store is a 'shared system resource' is an interpretation the control makes explicit and 800-53 does not.
IAM-06.residual: Per-session independent security context for agent memory and context, including between sessions of the same user. Agent context is not named as a shared resource.

mappings.why: Prevent unintended information transfer via shared system resources.
Separation of information flows by type.
No session may exercise access authorised to another.

IAM-07.fit_basis: Transitive delegation depth limits and chain reconstruction have no 800-53 analogue. Only the audit-attribution fragment maps. Cross-check addition: chain reconstruction maps to SA-8.22 and AU-3; the depth bound and blocking of downstream proxying still have no analogue.
IAM-07.residual: Maximum delegation depth (two hops) and blocking downstream proxying of the agent's identity at the infrastructure layer. Reconstructing the chain with originating identity is now mapped to SA-8.22 and AU-3. 800-53 has no concept of transitive delegation (cf. OAuth token exchange / on-behalf-of).

mappings.why: Accountability and traceability design principle: trace security-relevant actions to the entity on whose behalf they are taken; covers the chain-reconstruction clause.
Audit records identifying subjects; covers only the chain-reconstruction fragment.
Non-repudiation of actions performed by a process on behalf of an individual.
Limiting what a delegated principal can do; does not address depth.

cross_check.summary: NIST sources want attenuation and cryptographic traceability along delegation chains; none states a depth limit.

evidence.quote: each agent in a delegation chain has fewer permissions than its predecessor
remain cryptographically traceable to the entity originating the agentic instruction
trace security-relevant actions (i.e., subject-object interactions) to the entity on whose behalf the action is being taken

not_found: No maximum delegation depth or hop limit in SP 2400-102, IR 8596, the NCCoE summary or IR 8621 (terms searched: maximum depth, hop limit, max hops, delegation depth, depth limit: 0 hits). 'Hops' appears once, describing the problem.
cross_check.note: Rating unchanged: novel relative to 800-53 as written. NIST's attenuation and traceability goals are already in IAM-02, IAM-07 (traceability) and IAM-08.

IAM-08.fit_basis: Minimum-scope credentials and revocation are AC-6, IA-5 and AC-3.8. Per-tool token minting and cascade revocation through a delegation chain are not stated.
IAM-08.residual: Short-lived per-tool tokens and revocation that cascades through the delegation chain.

mappings.why: Least privilege applied to credential scope.
Authenticator lifecycle.
Revocation of access authorizations when attributes change.

IAM-09.fit_basis: Access enforcement and execution isolation cover the intent. 800-53 has no explicit multi-tenancy control and nothing on IDOR-class tenant scoping.
IAM-09.residual: Server-side tenant-ID scoping on every execution, tool call and query, with no user-controlled object IDs able to bypass it (CWE-639). 800-53 has no explicit multi-tenancy control.

mappings.why: Enforce authorizations for logical access; tenant scoping is an access-control decision.
Separate execution domains; covers 'cross-tenant execution impossible'.
Logical separation of information flows between tenants.
Cross-tenant leakage via shared resources.

IAM-10.fit_basis: Narrowing a subagent's privilege dynamically based on the taint of the data it processes is an information-flow-control model. 800-53 supplies vocabulary (labels, flows, least privilege) but no such control. Note the SI-20 'Tainting' name collision. Cross-check: SP 2400-102 describes dynamic taint tracking as a research defence, not a control.
IAM-10.residual: Taint-marking untrusted records at ingestion and dynamically narrowing the subagent's grants while it processes tainted data. AC-16, AC-4 and AC-6 supply labelling, flow and least-privilege vocabulary only.

mappings.why: Least privilege; here dynamic and task-scoped.
Associating security attributes with information; a taint mark is such an attribute.
Dynamically associate attributes as information is created and combined: the vocabulary for taint marking at ingestion and propagation.
Information flow enforcement between trust zones.
Dynamic information flow control: enforcement that changes with conditions, including detection of potentially harmful events.
Attribute-based access control is the mechanism class that could enforce it.
Name collision. SI-20 'Tainting' embeds markers to detect exfiltration of organisational data. IAM-10 taint-tracks inbound untrusted data to constrain privilege. Different concept.

qualifiers.subject: both
qualifiers.description: Do not treat these as equivalent on the strength of the shared word 'taint'. A reviewer mapping by title or keyword would wrongly report IAM-10 as covered by SI-20.

cross_check.summary: NIST describes taint tracking as a research defence and NCCoE commenters want authorization to tighten on untrusted data; no control.

evidence.quote: FIDES [121] applies dynamic taint tracking with confidentiality and integrity labels to regulate data flows
restrict the generality of the agent, and in most cases induce utility loss

evidence.where: Direct and Indirect Prompt Injection (commenter position)
evidence.quote: might even need to change whenever an agent operates on untrusted data

not_found: No NIST control or guideline requires privilege to narrow with taint. SP 2400-102 presents information-flow control as an approach that 'future work should investigate'.
cross_check.note: Rating unchanged. The cost caveat (utility loss) is worth carrying into IAM-10's L3/L4 guidance.

TP-01.fit_basis: A registry of approved, versioned tools is a component inventory plus allow-by-exception. Assumes each agent-callable tool is treated as a component or external service; the unit of inventory is a judgement the control leaves to the implementer.

mappings.why: Inventory of system components that accurately reflects the system; an unregistered tool is an inventory gap.
Deny-all, permit-by-exception for what may execute: the registry is the allowlist.
Detect unauthorized components and act on them: covers the unregistered-tool blind-spot clause.
Security approval before a tool enters service is configuration change control.

TP-02.fit_basis: Per-agent authorisation to invoke a tool is access enforcement and least privilege; the tool authenticating the calling agent is service authentication. Depends on a distinct agent identity (IAM-01); see the IA-2 tension recorded there.

mappings.why: Enforce approved authorizations for access to the tool.
Only the tools the agent's function requires.
Uniquely identify and authenticate the calling service or application before communications.
Attribute-based policy is one way to bind agent to permitted tools.

TP-03.fit_basis: Rate limiting, payload validation, schema enforcement and audit logging at the API edge are each standard 800-53 mechanisms. SC-7.17 (enforce protocol formats) is a good match for schema enforcement.

mappings.why: Check validity of inputs: payload validation.
Monitor and control communications at managed interfaces: the gateway is the managed interface.
Enforce adherence to protocol formats: schema enforcement.
Rate limiting as denial-of-service protection.
Audit record generation for gateway events.

TP-04.fit_basis: Structural validation of tool output maps to SI-15 (output consistent with expected content) and SI-10. The injection-prevention intent does not carry over: SI-10.6's mechanism assumes data and code can be separated, which an LLM context cannot do.
TP-04.residual: Sanitising tool output against instruction content that the model will follow (tool-output prompt injection). 800-53's injection controls rely on parameterized interfaces or escaping; natural-language instructions inside a context window cannot be escaped that way.

mappings.why: Validate output from programs to ensure it is consistent with expected content: structural validation of tool output.
From the agent's side, tool output is an information input to be checked for validity.
Prevent untrusted data injections: right intent, wrong mechanism for an LLM context. See qualifier.
Restrict inputs to trusted sources and approved formats; covers the structural half only.

qualifiers.subject: target
qualifiers.description: SI-10.6 is met by parameterized interfaces or output escaping, which separate data from code. A model reading tool output has no such separation: instructions and data share one channel. SI-10.6 can be satisfied literally (every conventional parser is protected) while tool-output injection into the model is unaddressed.

TP-05.fit_basis: Signed, attested, gated pipelines that deploy an agent are developer configuration management and software integrity verification. The agent is simply the deployed software. 'Attestation' is SLSA/in-toto vocabulary; SR-4.3 and SI-7.15 cover the same verification intent.

mappings.why: Developer configuration management with integrity control over changes.
Cryptographic authentication of software components before installation.
Prevent installation of components without verification of a digital signature.
Enable integrity verification of software components.
Validate that a received component is genuine and not altered: the attestation clause.
Security validation gates in the pipeline are developer testing and evaluation.

TP-06.fit_basis: Continuous vulnerability scanning of libraries is RA-5 and SI-2. Models and model registries as scannable dependency artifacts, and automated blocking on critical findings, are not stated.
TP-06.residual: Treating models and model registries as dependencies to be scanned (e.g. serialized model files that execute code on load), and an automated block on critical findings. RA-5 requires scanning and timely remediation, not a blocking gate.

mappings.why: Monitor and scan for vulnerabilities in the system and hosted applications; remediate.
Identify, report and correct flaws: the remediation half.
Automated vulnerability analysis in development, where the organisation is the developer.
Identify and address weaknesses in supply chain elements.
Malicious code protection is the nearest analogue for malicious model artifacts.

TP-07.fit_basis: BORDERLINE partial/novel. Threat modelling and risk assessment are umbrella controls under which tool-composition analysis could sit, but nothing in 800-53 asks for it. Rated partial only because the generic analysis exists; confidence is low.
TP-07.residual: Combinatorial analysis of registered tools for escape, privilege-escalation and exfiltration chains, and explicit risk acceptance of escape-class chains. 800-53 has no concept of analysing capability composition across components.

mappings.why: Risk assessment identifying threats and vulnerabilities; generic umbrella.
Threat modelling and vulnerability analyses during development; applies where the organisation develops the agent system.
Impact analysis before a change: adding a tool to the registry is such a change.
Separation of duties addresses conflicting capability combinations in people; the analogy to tools is loose.

TP-08.fit_basis: An endpoint allow-list at the agent gateway that excludes control-plane APIs is deny-by-default with exceptions; treating blocked calls as compromise indicators is monitoring and alerting. Largely the same as EE-02 viewed from the gateway.

mappings.why: Deny communications by default and allow by exception: the endpoint allow-list at the gateway.
Boundary protection at the managed interface.
Alert on defined indications of compromise: a non-tool API call is one.
Blocked calls are logged.

TP-09.fit_basis: Least functionality and secure defaults state the principle. The specific failure (an agent framework reflecting over internal helpers and exposing them as callable tools) is an agent-era implementation hazard 800-53 does not name.
TP-09.residual: Prohibiting attribute-based, reflection-based or discovery-based registration of internal functions and SDK helpers as agent-callable tools; every callable must be explicitly declared.

mappings.why: Configure the system to provide only essential capabilities.
Allow-by-exception for what may be invoked.
Secure defaults: nothing callable unless explicitly enabled.
Registry is the inventory (see TP-01).

TP-10.fit_basis: Default-deny listeners, closing unneeded ports and protocols, and session authenticity are all 800-53. Treating the agent platform's loopback gateway as an attack surface, origin-bound tokens against cross-site WebSocket hijack, and agent-initiated service binding are not.
TP-10.residual: Origin-bound gateway tokens that cannot be read from browser context (cross-site WebSocket hijack resistance), and detecting and blocking service binding initiated by the agent itself. 800-53 assumes administrators, not the agent, open listeners.

mappings.why: Prohibit or restrict functions, ports, protocols and services.
Only allow incoming communications from defined sources: the inbound deny-by-default policy.
Deny by default, allow by exception.
Protect session authenticity, including against session hijacking: nearest home for origin-bound session handling.
Detect unauthorized local, network and remote connections.
Protect authenticators: covers the token-not-readable clause.

TP-11.fit_basis: The core is that content an agent perceives (rendered pages, uploaded documents, hidden text) becomes a command channel, and that origin isolation must hold for an agent acting across sites. 800-53 has no vocabulary for untrusted instruction-bearing content or same-origin policy. Only fragments (mobile code, detonation, input validation) apply.
TP-11.residual: Classifying rendered content as untrusted, stripping imperceptible instruction vectors before agent action, preserving origin and content isolation for an agent acting across sites, and keeping credential material out of the browser/session layer. No 800-53 control is built on content-as-command.

mappings.why: Restrict inputs to trusted sources: the untrusted-content classification, without the instruction-stripping.
Mobile code control and monitoring: covers scripts in pages, not hidden text instructions.
Detonation chambers for untrusted attachments: relevant to document-upload sanitisation.
Process isolation for the rendering component; does not address origin isolation.

cross_check.summary: SP 2400-102 documents instructions injected visually into browser and computer-use agents; no NIST control addresses origin or content isolation.

evidence.quote: adversaries can inject instructions visually
agents clicked on adversarial pop-ups in 86% of cases on average

not_found: 'same-origin', 'origin isolation', 'cross-origin' and 'content isolation' return 0 hits across SP 2400-102, IR 8596, the NCCoE summary and IR 8621.

TP-12.fit_basis: BORDERLINE partial/novel. Session authenticity and a reference monitor give vocabulary for 'dispatch must be mediated and session events must be authentic'. Cryptographically bound model-turn provenance for tool calls, and approvals bound to exact tool name and arguments, have no 800-53 analogue.
TP-12.residual: Verifying that a tool call originated from an authorised model turn (session, turn, model signature) before dispatch; binding approval records to the exact tool name and arguments; verifying approvals against the human channel, never against agent-writable session history. 800-53 does not treat a model as an authorised source of instructions.

mappings.why: Protect authenticity of sessions including against insertion of false information: forged session events.
Reference monitor: tamperproof, always invoked; the dispatch layer is this.
Irrefutable evidence an action was performed by an identified party; relevant to approval records.
Enforcement of authorizations at dispatch.
Integrity of the events and history the dispatcher trusts.

TP-13.fit_basis: Governing software installation and validating component provenance are CM-11 and SR-4. The trigger (install commands lifted from ingested documentation) and the checks (does the package exist in the registry, does the namespace belong to the vendor, has the documented domain expired) are not stated.
TP-13.residual: Refusing to treat ingested documentation (README, llms.txt) as an authoritative install script; registry-existence, namespace-ownership and domain-expiry checks before install; treating dangling references as findings.

mappings.why: Policy governing software installation, with enforcement and monitoring.
Document, monitor and maintain valid provenance of components.
Operator allowlist of authorized software.
Validate a received component is genuine and not altered.
Signed-component verification, where the package ecosystem provides signatures.

TP-14.fit_basis: Signed immutable payloads and provenance map well to CM-14, SI-7.15 and SR-4. The payload being natural-language instructions, and runtime-fetchable instruction channels being a C2 path invisible to tool-call monitoring, are not addressed.
TP-14.residual: Fixing instruction content at install time and prohibiting runtime-fetchable instruction channels; capability-scoped skill privileges below the agent's own identity; behavioural baseline with quarantine on drift. 800-53's code-signing vocabulary assumes the signed artifact is code, not instructions.

mappings.why: Prevent installation without verification of a recognised digital signature.
Cryptographically authenticate components before installation.
Provenance end to end, publisher to artifact.
Skill privileges scoped to declared capability, not the agent's full identity.
Prevent download and execution of defined mobile code: relates to the runtime-fetch prohibition.
Component authenticity; framed around counterfeit, so only loosely applicable to malicious marketplace listings.

TP-15.fit_basis: Running untrusted code in an isolated execution domain is SC-39, CM-7.6 and SC-44. The control's substance is a negative assertion (a denylist in-process sandbox is not a boundary) that 800-53 does not make, so an assessor could accept a weak sandbox as satisfying SC-39.
TP-15.residual: The explicit determination that denylist or blocklist in-process sandboxes are code-execution surfaces, not security boundaries; classifying any unavoidable in-process sandbox as high-risk with automated blocking; a mandatory alternative-evaluation gate at higher maturity.

mappings.why: Separate execution domain per process: an in-process sandbox shares the host process, so arguably fails. See qualifier.
Execute in a confined physical or virtual environment with limited privileges.
Detonation chamber: isolated sandbox for executing untrusted code.
Boundary mechanisms isolating components; see EE-01.

qualifiers.subject: both
qualifiers.description: To make SC-39 equivalent to TP-15, an assessor must interpret 'execution domain' as OS- or VM-enforced separation and reject in-process interpreter gates. SC-39 does not say so; an implementation using a hardened interpreter could be argued to pass SC-39 while failing TP-15.

TP-16.fit_basis: A server-supplied string reaching an OS launch primitive is classic command injection: SI-10 and SI-10.6 fit this case well, since a launch path is a real parser boundary. The agent-era residue is MCP/OAuth metadata as the untrusted input and model-influenced server definitions registering launch commands.
TP-16.residual: Origin-binding of OAuth authorization endpoints to the configured server; validating and allowlisting launch commands registered through tool or server definitions, including those a prompt-injected model can influence; assuming later compromise of a previously benign server.

mappings.why: Prevent untrusted data injections via parameterized interfaces: the launch path is a genuine data/code boundary, unlike TP-04.
Validate inputs: peer-supplied protocol metadata.
Restrict inputs to trusted sources and approved formats: origin-bound endpoints.
Deny-all, permit-by-exception for programs that may execute: allowlisted launch commands.
Prevent program execution per policy.
Managed information exchange with connected systems; onboarding and reconnection of tool servers.

MS-01.fit_basis: Model weights are information at rest and in transit; SC-28.1, SC-12 and SC-8.1 cover encryption and key management, and the HSM-backed requirement is an ODP choice under SC-12. The only interpretation needed is that weights are a protected information type. Remote attestation for edge deployments has no exact analogue; SI-7 integrity verification is the nearest and is recorded at low confidence.

mappings.why: Cryptographic protection of information at rest: weights at rest.
Key establishment and management; HSM-backed management is an organisation-defined requirement.
Cryptographic protection during transmission: weights in transit.
Determining and implementing the cryptography required for each use.
Integrity verification; nearest home for attestation of weights on edge devices.

MS-02.fit_basis: BORDERLINE partial/novel. Dataset versioning, access control and provenance map to SI-7, SR-4 and AC-3. Poisoning is different in kind: crafted samples that arrive through an authorised path and pass format checks are not an unauthorised change, so integrity controls do not detect them.
MS-02.residual: Statistical and semantic detection of poisoned samples (anomaly detection, drift monitoring) and retraining triggered by integrity findings. 800-53 integrity controls detect unauthorised modification, not authorised-but-malicious data.

mappings.why: Provenance of data and components: lineage for training datasets.
Integrity verification of information; catches tampering after approval, not poisoning before it. See qualifier.
Access controls on training data.
Validate inputs at ingestion; covers the L2 format checks only.

qualifiers.subject: target
qualifiers.description: SI-7 can be satisfied in full while training data is poisoned: it detects unauthorised changes to information, and a poisoned sample inserted through a legitimate ingestion path is not one. Meeting MS-02 needs statistical validation in addition to SI-7.

MS-03.fit_basis: Provenance and integrity of weights, ML libraries, training infrastructure and deployment tooling are the subject of the SR family, with models treated as system components. Compare TP-06, rated partial because it also requires treating models as scannable dependencies and automated blocking, which MS-03 does not.

mappings.why: Process to identify and address weaknesses in supply chain elements.
Document, monitor and maintain provenance of components and associated data.
Validate that a received component is genuine and not altered: pre-trained models from public hubs.
Assess and review suppliers, including public model repositories.
Cryptographic authentication of components before installation.
Signed components, where the model ecosystem provides signatures.
Organisation-wide supply chain risk management strategy.

MS-04.fit_basis: Reclassified from novel while cross-checking against NIST. The reason is the control's own text: its objective and maturity indicators are mostly testing activities (a prompt-injection test suite, an adversarial CI/CD gate, quarterly red-teaming, proxy-layer output guardrails), which CA-8, CA-8.2, SA-11.5 and SI-15 cover. NIST's predictive-AI overlay outline also lists CA-8, SA-11(05), SI-10 and SI-10(05), but it concerns predictive AI, gives no reasons for its selections, and says its list is incomplete, so it is corroboration at most. What 800-53 cannot express is the outcome: that a model actually resists injection.
MS-04.residual: Model-level resistance to prompt injection cannot be specified or verified by any 800-53 control (SP 2400-102 itself says current mitigations do not offer full protection), and sanitising imperceptible content (zero-opacity, sub-pixel, DOM-hidden text) before reasoning has no 800-53 home. 800-53 can require that adversarial testing is done, not that it succeeds.

mappings.why: Penetration testing: the periodic adversarial testing requirement. Also listed in NIST's predictive-AI overlay outline.
Input validation; covers structural checks, not instruction content.
Injection prevention; mechanism assumes parameterized interfaces. See qualifier and TP-04.
Restrict inputs to trusted sources and approved formats.
Policy filters on content, with hidden content named in guidance.
Red-team exercises: the L3/L4 red-teaming requirement.
Developer penetration testing: the pre-deployment adversarial test requirement. Also listed in NIST's predictive-AI overlay outline.
Output filtering: covers the L3 proxy-layer output guardrails only.

qualifiers.subject: target
qualifiers.description: SI-10.6 is met by parameterized interfaces or output escaping, which separate data from code. A model reads instructions and data in one channel, so SI-10.6 can be satisfied for every conventional parser while prompt injection is untouched.

cross_check.summary: Rated novel before the cross-check; on re-reading, most of the control is testing activity that 800-53 already covers, so downgraded to partial. NIST's predictive-AI overlay outline corroborates weakly.

evidence.where: Overlay control list and SI-03(08) discussion
evidence.quote: much in the way that SQL injection attacks are identified
CA-08, Penetration Testing
application designers may design systems with the assumption that prompt injection attacks are possible
adaptive attacks have bypassed many published jailbreak and prompt injection defenses that initially reported strong robustness

cross_check.note: This downgrade rests mainly on the control's own maturity indicators, not on NIST. The earlier novel rating weighted the 'model resists injection' narrative over those testing requirements. NIST's overlay outline is for predictive AI; its SI-03(08) tailoring uses an SQL-injection analogy, but SI-3.8's statement concerns operating-system commands through a kernel interface, so I did not map to it.

MS-05.fit_basis: Output guardrails (PII filtering, toxicity, per-agent bounds) are information output filtering: SI-15 validates output against expected content and AC-4.8 enforces content filters. Both were written for software whose 'expected content' is a specification. Overlaps DS-06.
MS-05.residual: Semantic output bounds (safety, scope, domain-appropriate advice) and bounds adjusted dynamically from production telemetry. SI-15 presumes the expected content can be specified.

mappings.why: Validate output to ensure it is consistent with expected content.
Information flow control using content filters, with a defined response to filter failure.
Information flow enforcement between the model and its consumers.
Monitoring of outputs in production.

MS-06.fit_basis: Inventory, versioning and lineage of models are component inventory (CM-8), baseline configuration (CM-2) and provenance (SR-4), with retirement covered by CM-8.1 updates on removal. Requires treating a model as a system component, as with TP-01.

mappings.why: Inventory of system components that accurately reflects the system: 'what models do we have?'
Update the inventory on installation, removal and update: covers retirement.
Provenance and lineage of a component.
Baseline configuration under configuration control: versioning.
Inventory of organisational systems.
Developer configuration management.

MS-07.fit_basis: Requires the evaluation environment to be indistinguishable from production from the model's perspective. 800-53 applies the opposite pressure: CM-4.1 and SA-3.1 require test environments to be separate from and protected relative to production, and nothing asks that they be undetectable. The control treats the model as an adversary that games evaluations.
MS-07.residual: Indistinguishability of API endpoints, data formats, latency, error handling and credential lifetimes between evaluation and production, with divergence checks treated as an incident signal. 800-53 has no concept of a system under test that detects the test.

mappings.why: Analyse changes in a separate test environment. See qualifier.
Protect preproduction environments commensurate with risk.

qualifiers.subject: both
qualifiers.description: CM-4.1 requires a separate test environment; MS-07 additionally requires that environment to be indistinguishable from production. Satisfying CM-4.1 with a clearly labelled, differently configured test environment is exactly what lets a model detect evaluation (see EE-04).

cross_check.summary: Not addressed. SP 2400-102 records models escaping test environments but excludes it from scope; NIST's overlay outline selects separation, not indistinguishability.

evidence.quote: models have reached the internet from test environments and gained unauthorized access to third-party systems
are thus outside the scope of the taxonomy
Separate Test Environments

not_found: 'evaluation awareness', 'situational awareness', 'sandbagging' and 'indistinguishable from production' return 0 hits in SP 2400-102, IR 8596, the NCCoE summary and IR 8621.
cross_check.note: Rating unchanged. The CM-4.1 tension recorded as a qualifier stands: NIST's own outline selects the separation direction.

MS-08.fit_basis: The mechanisms are standard: signed metadata, service authentication, response validation, trusted registry, fail-closed authentication, alerting on writes. MCP is a protocol-layer attack surface 800-53 does not name, and tool metadata is instruction-bearing content, which is the trigger half seen in TP-16 and TP-12.
MS-08.residual: Treating MCP tool definitions and discovery metadata as security-relevant content to be signed and validated against a known-good schema; monitoring model-originated writes to execution-bearing locations and publication channels; a protocol-level rule against downgrading to anonymous sessions and against default gateway credentials.

mappings.why: Uniquely identify and authenticate services before communications: MCP gateway authentication.
Cryptographic authentication of components: signed tool metadata.
Validate responses against known-good schemas.
Authenticator management includes changing default authenticators before first use: the no-default-credentials clause.
Fail to a known state: authentication failure must not downgrade to anonymous.
Signed components.
Alert on defined indications of compromise: model-originated writes to execution-bearing locations.
Provenance for the trusted registry.

MS-09.fit_basis: Requires that content an agent acts on is perceptually equivalent to what the human approver sees, and binds approvals to a snapshot of the rendered content. This protects the integrity of the human-in-the-loop channel itself. 800-53 has no human-approval-of-action control (see IAM-03), so nothing addresses the fidelity of what the approver is shown.
MS-09.residual: Stripping or flagging imperceptible content (zero-opacity, sub-pixel, off-screen, DOM-hidden) before reasoning, and binding each approval to a rendering-fidelity snapshot of the exact content acted on.

mappings.why: Content filters, with hidden content named in guidance.
Irrefutable evidence of what was approved; the approval record would need to include the rendered content.
Human reviews under defined conditions: the approval step whose fidelity MS-09 protects.

cross_check.summary: NIST documents visual injection and warns about approval fatigue; nothing addresses whether the approver sees what the agent acted on.

evidence.quote: adversaries can inject instructions visually
cryptographically signed intent or flight plans
relying too heavily on HITL mechanisms introduces a severe risk of consent fatigue

not_found: 'rendering fidelity', 'perceptually equivalent', 'what the human sees' and 'approval snapshot' return 0 hits in the four documents searched.
cross_check.note: Rating unchanged. NCCoE's signed 'flight plan' binds an approval to a decomposed task list, which is related to MS-09's approval snapshot but binds to intent, not to what was rendered.

MS-10.fit_basis: Access control, integrity protection and audit of memory writes map to AC-3, SI-7.6 and AU-12. As with MS-02, an authenticated agent writing a malicious memory is an authorised write, so integrity controls do not catch it, and the effect persists across software patches.
MS-10.residual: Treating persistent agent memory (vector stores, learned patterns, histories) as a behaviour-steering store; retrieval-layer filtering of flagged entries; a post-incident audit-and-clean procedure for the store itself; red-team testing of poisoning persistence.

mappings.why: Authenticated, authorised writes to the memory store.
Cryptographic mechanisms to detect unauthorized changes to information: tamper-evident memory.
Audit record generation for memory writes.
Write-once media; loose analogue for append-only or immutable snapshots.
Anomaly detection on memory writes.
Eradication step of incident handling, applied to the memory store.

MS-11.fit_basis: Producer authentication for log and alert streams maps to AU-10.1, IA-9 and SI-10.5. The control's core is different: an agent that reads logs or alerts will follow instructions embedded in them, so an operational feed becomes a command channel. That trigger has no 800-53 analogue (compare TP-11).
MS-11.residual: Treating log, alert and observability content as untrusted instruction-bearing input; independent non-log verification before a log-triggered action; flagging agent actions whose proximate cause was a log entry.

mappings.why: Restrict inputs to trusted sources: authenticated producers only.
Bind the identity of the information producer to the information.
Authenticate services before communications: ingestion pipelines authenticate producers.
Uniquely identify and authenticate source points for information transfer.
Monitoring; agent actions traced to a log entry would be flagged here.

MS-12.fit_basis: Baseline validation and drift alerting for tool metadata map to CM-2 and SI-7; cache isolation across authentication contexts maps to AC-3 and SC-4. Instruction-bearing discovery metadata is again the trigger half.
MS-12.residual: Length-limiting and screening MCP instructions and tool descriptions for instruction content; isolating them from the trusted system prompt; verifying, not trusting, server-declared cache scope claims.

mappings.why: Detect unauthorized changes to tool metadata against an approved baseline.
Cache entries served only within the authentication context that produced them.
Operator-approved baseline of tool metadata.
Prevent information transfer via shared resources: shared caches.
Cryptographic protection: signed cached metadata.
Restrict inputs to approved formats; covers length limits.

MS-13.fit_basis: Signed or chained transcripts are audit-record integrity (AU-9.3), non-repudiation (AU-10) and session authenticity (SC-23). The unusual feature is that the transcript is something the model itself reasons over as ground truth, so its integrity is a safety property and not only an evidence property.
MS-13.residual: Signing model outputs with a per-session key held outside the harness; verifying every stored response on read before the agent reasons over it; refusing confidence-gated action from an unverified transcript.

mappings.why: Cryptographic protection of the integrity of audit information.
Irrefutable evidence of what the model said.
Protect the authenticity of sessions, including insertion of false information.
Write-once media; loose analogue for an append-only transcript.
Cryptographic detection of unauthorized change.

MS-14.fit_basis: Using the agent as a propagation vector for its own injected instructions (a prompt worm) has no 800-53 analogue. SI-3 names worms but concerns malicious code, and SC-7.9 extrusion detection concerns traffic that threatens external systems, not instruction-bearing natural language.
MS-14.residual: Fingerprinting instruction-bearing input and matching it against outbound content before publish; quarantine and human sign-off on suspected echoes; blast-radius caps per propagation hop; worm-emulation drills.

mappings.why: Malicious code protection; worms are named, but as code.
Detect and deny outgoing traffic posing a threat to external systems.
Output filtering for content inconsistent with expected output.
Content filters on information flows.

cross_check.summary: SP 2400-102 documents self-propagating injections and lists inter-agent firewalls; its mitigations do not include outbound-content screening.

evidence.quote: certain malicious prompts could serve as worms
self-replicating prompt injection attacks that spread malicious instructions across interconnected agents
Firewalls placed on inter-agent channels enforce constraints at each communication channel

not_found: 'fingerprint' and 'quarantin*' return 0 hits in SP 2400-102, IR 8596, the NCCoE summary and IR 8621. §3.5.4's indirect-injection mitigations (training, detection, input filtering, spotlighting, privilege separation) do not include screening of outbound content.
cross_check.note: Rating unchanged. Absence from a draft attack taxonomy is not absence from NIST's thinking; SP 2400-102 says mitigations for multi-agent threats are 'an understudied area'.

MS-15.fit_basis: Cross-tenant memory isolation is access enforcement and separation of information flows, as with IAM-09. Pooled vector stores add a failure mode with no 800-53 vocabulary: similarity retrieval crosses ownership boundaries without any exploit. Keyword search of Rev 5.2 finds no 'tenant'.
MS-15.residual: Hard post-retrieval ownership gating (similarity is not admissibility); treating any cross-tenant hit as an alarm; a tenant or namespace key that is never a model-controllable tool argument; fail-closed refusal when ownership cannot be verified.

mappings.why: Enforce authorizations at retrieval and write: ownership gating.
Logical separation of information flows between tenants.
Prevent unintended information transfer via shared resources: a pooled index.
Least common mechanism: design principle against shared mechanisms.
Minimized sharing.

DS-01.fit_basis: Automated classification at ingestion that drives downstream handling is attribute association (AC-16), with dynamic association as information is created (AC-16.1) and categorisation (RA-2). Assumes the ODPs name the organisation's classification scheme.

mappings.why: Associate security and privacy attributes with information in storage, process and transmission.
Dynamically associate attributes as information is created and combined: classification at ingestion.
Security categorization of the information the system processes.
Flow decisions based on the attributes.

DS-02.fit_basis: Encryption of data in transit between user, agent, model and tool endpoints is SC-8 and SC-8.1. 'Data extraction' is read here as interception. If it is read as model or training-data extraction through queries, that is not covered (see DS-06).

mappings.why: Protect confidentiality and integrity of transmitted information.
Cryptographic mechanisms during transmission.
Cryptography required for each use.
Key management.
Session authenticity.

DS-03.fit_basis: Retention, disposal, encryption at rest and prevention of cross-session leakage map to SI-12, SI-12.3, SC-28.1 and SC-4. Persistent agent memory as a cross-session aggregation point is not named.
DS-03.residual: Detecting cross-session aggregation of sensitive data in agent memory, and per-agent memory scoping as a design requirement. MP-6 media sanitisation concerns media at disposal, not purging stored context.

mappings.why: Cryptographic protection of information at rest: encrypted memory.
Manage and retain information per requirements: retention policy.
Disposal of information after the retention period: automated purging.
Prevent information transfer via shared resources: cross-session leakage.
Media sanitization; literal media, loose analogue for purging memory.

DS-04.fit_basis: 800-53 minimisation is scoped to PII (SI-12.1, PT-2, PM-25). DS-04 applies to all data exposed to a model, retrieved or stored, as least privilege for data.
DS-04.residual: Minimising non-PII sensitive data exposed to the model's context, and per-task retrieval scoping. AC-6 least privilege applies to accounts and processes, not to the volume of data placed in a context window.

mappings.why: Limit PII elements processed in the information life cycle.
Restrict processing of PII to what is authorized.
Least privilege, applied to data access.
Least privilege design principle.
Minimise PII used in testing, training and research.

DS-05.fit_basis: The privacy families (PT, SI-12, PM-25) cover consent, purpose and retention for personal data used in training. Lineage maps loosely to provenance. Scope is PII-only. How these align with the Privacy Act 1988 is not assessed here.
DS-05.residual: Lineage from source through preprocessing to training for all training data, not only PII; verifying consent for personal data used to train a model; machine unlearning (removing a record's influence from a trained model); continuous training-data audit. 800-53 disposal controls act on stored information, not on a model derived from it.

mappings.why: Consent to processing of PII prior to collection.
Identify and restrict PII processing purposes.
Retention of information.
Minimise PII used in research, testing and training.
Provenance of data.
Data governance body.

DS-06.fit_basis: PII and sensitive-data scanning of output is output filtering (SI-15) and content flow filtering (AC-4.8). Leakage of memorised training data and system prompts has no analogue: nothing in 800-53 refers to a model reproducing its inputs. Overlaps MS-05.
DS-06.residual: Detecting memorised training data and system-prompt fragments in model output, and memorisation testing in CI/CD. SI-15 validates output against 'expected content', which presumes the expected content can be specified.

mappings.why: Validate output to ensure consistency with expected content.
Content filters on information flows.
Monitor for evidence of unauthorized disclosure of information.
Prevent exfiltration.

DS-07.fit_basis: Agent-authored artifacts entering the same integrity pipeline as third-party ones maps to SA-10, SI-7.15, CM-14 and SI-3. Out-of-band approval for publication that the agent cannot invoke is separation of duties (AC-5) and dual authorization (AC-3.2) applied to an agent. Same gap as IAM-03.
DS-07.residual: Publication as an egress event requiring approval the agent can neither trigger nor satisfy, and publication credentials unreachable through the ordinary tool path. 800-53 separation of duties is written for people.

mappings.why: Separation of duties: the agent cannot approve its own publication.
Developer configuration management with integrity control.
Cryptographic authentication before installation.
Access restrictions for change: writes to execution-bearing locations.
Dual authorization for defined actions.
Signed components.
Malware scanning of artifacts.

DS-08.fit_basis: Egress allow-listing, exfiltration prevention and covert-channel analysis are all in 800-53 (SC-7.5, SC-7.10, SC-31, SI-4.18). Agent-era emergent channels fall in the gaps: a rendered image tag or link unfurl is fetched by the user's client or a third-party service, outside the network boundary SC-7.5 governs.
DS-08.residual: Enumerating client-side and third-party fetch channels (image rendering, link unfurl, webhook preview) as egress sinks; payload-blind hard allow-lists rather than content classifiers; DNS egress restricted to allow-listed resolvers with queried names inspected. SC-31 covers the analysis in principle, as a design-time covert channel analysis.

mappings.why: Deny by default, allow by exception: the destination allow-list.
Prevent exfiltration and test for it.
Covert channel analysis: finds channels not on the declared list.
Analyse outbound traffic for covert exfiltration.
Information flow enforcement to defined destinations.
Detect and deny outgoing traffic posing a threat.
Route traffic through authenticated proxies.

MIR-01.fit_basis: Structured, attributable activity records correlated to the initiating session are audit event selection, content and generation. Requires treating agent actions as auditable events and the agent as a subject in AU-3's identity element.

mappings.why: Identify the event types to be logged: every agent action.
Audit record content: type, time, location, source, outcome, identity.
Audit record generation.
Additional audit information: correlation to the initiating human session.
System-wide, time-correlated audit trail.
Session audit.

MIR-02.fit_basis: Per-agent behavioural baselines with deviation alerting are profile-based monitoring (SI-4.13) within system monitoring (SI-4). SI-4.13 is written for traffic and event patterns; applying it to agent action sequences is an extension, so 'direct' assumes that reading. Adversary-owned autonomous agents are an attacker class that SI-4 already addresses as attacks and indicators of attacks.

mappings.why: Develop profiles representing common traffic and event patterns and use them in monitoring.
Monitor to detect attacks and indicators of potential attacks.
Analyse anomalous or suspected adversarial behaviour.
Analyse outbound traffic anomalies; covers unexpected listener and binding events.
Review and analyse audit records for unusual activity.

MIR-03.fit_basis: Capturing sanitised prompt/response content is session audit (AU-14) with PII limiting in audit records (AU-3.3). AU-14 requires consultation with legal counsel, which is a real constraint on prompt logging.

mappings.why: Capture the content of a session, in consultation with legal counsel.
Limit PII in audit records to elements identified in the privacy risk assessment: the sanitisation half. See qualifier.
Audit record content.
Additional audit information: prompt and response.
Protect audit information.
Retention for after-the-fact investigation.

qualifiers.subject: both
qualifiers.description: A prompt/response log is itself a new high-sensitivity data store. AU-3.3 ties the PII elements retained to a privacy risk assessment, so MIR-03 cannot be treated as met without one.

MIR-04.fit_basis: 800-53 requires an incident response capability, plan, handling and testing (IR-4, IR-8, IR-3), and automated handling (IR-4.1) covers SOAR. It does not require playbooks per incident type.
MIR-04.residual: AI-specific scenarios (prompt-injection containment, model rollback, tool revocation, code-generation attack containment) as required playbook content. 800-53 requires the capability, not scenario coverage.

mappings.why: Incident handling: preparation, detection, containment, eradication, recovery.
Incident response plan.
Test the response capability: tabletop exercises.
Automated incident handling: SOAR integration.
Automatic disabling of the system on defined conditions.
Incident response training.

MIR-05.fit_basis: IR-6 requires reporting within a defined time to defined parties, and its ODPs can name SOCI Act, APRA CPS 234 and Notifiable Data Breaches deadlines; IR-6.1 covers automation. The mapping is structural: the 12 and 72-hour windows are Australian regulation, not 800-53 content.

mappings.why: Report incidents within a defined time to defined parties.
Automated reporting.
Breach handling, including notice to individuals and regulators.
Reporting triggers belong in the incident response plan.
Notification agreements with supply chain entities.

MIR-06.fit_basis: Immutable, integrity-protected audit storage with retention and after-the-fact reconstruction is AU-9, AU-9.1 to AU-9.3, AU-11 and AU-7. Reconstructing every prompt, tool call, data access and decision presumes MIR-01 and MIR-03 supply the content.

mappings.why: Protect audit information from modification and deletion.
Hardware-enforced write-once media.
Store audit records on a physically different system.
Cryptographic integrity protection of audit information.
Retain audit records to support after-the-fact investigations.
Audit reduction and reporting supporting after-the-fact investigation.
Session audit.

GRM-01.fit_basis: A chartered body with authority to approve deployments and oversee posture maps to the risk executive function (PM-29) and the authorization process (PM-10, CA-6). Direct only if the organisation's existing risk governance already takes AI systems in scope; many do not, and 800-53 does not require it.

mappings.why: Risk executive function with a senior accountable official.
Authorization to operate: approving agentic AI deployments.
Authorization process with designated roles.
Risk management strategy.
Data governance body; nearest named governance body, scoped to data.

GRM-02.fit_basis: Risk assessment, risk response and POA&M cover the register itself. The AI-specific additions (threat taxonomy, automated tripwires, an exercised kill switch) are not stated, though IR-4.5 and CM-8.3 are partial analogues.
GRM-02.residual: A dedicated AI threat taxonomy (model, tool, data, identity, pipeline), automated tripwires, and a single exercised kill-switch capability tested at least annually. IR-4.5 is a configurable automatic disable on detection, not an organisation-wide kill switch that is exercised.

mappings.why: Risk assessment: threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact.
Respond to findings in accordance with risk tolerance.
Plan of action and milestones: tracked to resolution.
Risk management strategy.
Automatic disabling of the system: closest to a kill switch.
Detect unauthorized components: unledgered-asset discovery.
Risk framing.

GRM-03.fit_basis: Defining what agents may do, assigning autonomy by risk tier and setting transparency obligations has no 800-53 counterpart. Keyword search of Rev 5.2 statements and guidance finds no 'ethic' or 'autonom'. PL-4 rules of behaviour is the nearest and is written for human users.
GRM-03.residual: A policy of acceptable agent conduct, risk-tiered autonomy levels, and agent transparency obligations, with technical enforcement at the tool gateway (L4).

mappings.why: Rules of behaviour: the nearest policy-of-conduct control. See qualifier.
Limits on autonomy realised as least privilege.
Privacy notice; transparency obligation, scoped to PII.

qualifiers.subject: target

evidence.quote: Organizations decide who is accountable for actions taken by autonomous systems

evidence.where: ID.RA-06 (Defend focus area: AI used for cyber defence)
evidence.quote: Define conditions for disabling AI autonomy during risk response
what actions can be automated, what actions require human authorization

not_found: 'risk tier', 'tiered autonomy', 'autonomy level' and 'autonomy tier' return 0 hits across the four documents searched.
cross_check.note: Rating unchanged but the weakest remaining novel call after MS-04: the concept is present in NIST drafts and the policy container exists in 800-53 (PL-4, AC-1). May soften to partial once an agent overlay is published.

GRM-04.fit_basis: Assessing external providers, binding them contractually and coordinating incident handling with them is SA-9, SR-3, SR-5, SR-6 and SA-4. Right-to-audit is not named in 800-53 but falls under SA-9 oversight and SR-6 assessment. Rated direct on the assumption that ODPs cover model providers, tool providers and evaluation-harness vendors; the v1.5 additions (agent-speed adversary playbooks, harness isolation assurance per EE-08) are content the organisation must add.

GRM-05.fit_basis: Mapping controls to the regulations that apply and reporting compliance status on a cadence is continuous monitoring (CA-7, PM-31) and control assessment (CA-2); baseline selection and tailoring (PL-10, PL-11) is the mapping step. Australian regulators are ODP content.

mappings.why: Continuous monitoring with defined metrics and reporting.
Organisation-wide continuous monitoring strategy.
Control assessments and reporting of results.
Measures of performance, monitored and reported.
Select a control baseline: selecting the applicable requirements.
Tailor the baseline.

GRM-06.fit_basis: Reporting security measures, open findings (POA&M) and risk responses to senior management is PM-6, CA-5 and RA-7. Board-level, non-technical presentation and per-pillar maturity scores are not specified.
GRM-06.residual: Per-pillar maturity scoring for non-technical audiences. 800-53 baselines are met or not met per control and define no maturity ladder.
